23013.d:
Another year has begun. I love the boundaries of things. Like the border between years, the border between night and morning, day and night always fascinate us. When the year changes, I am certainly a different person than I was yesterday, but I am not sure that I have really changed. Am I really growing and changing for the better?
　It seems that the world does not always change for the better. I live in Japan, and in 2022 alone, there were many sad incidents. Every time I watch the news, I am disturbed. This is very sad.
　I am very, very small. I still don't know what kind of power I have, and even if I did, its impact on the world would be minute. I am building a staircase today. It is something that tries to see the boundary between something and something else, and connects them together so that they can come and go. The boundary will not be represented by a single line, but will be a vague gradation. Even with such uncertainty, I want to look at the heart of something that has changed or is about to change. I pray. I pray that even in the midst of so much sadness, there will be a little time for peace of mind. I pray that, as time goes by, we will be able to look at these sad events with a peaceful gaze. I want to build a staircase in my soul so that I can look through it.

23089.d:
This piece began with an attempt to generate rippling patterns that imitate an ocean surface, but evolved into a wider exploration of wave interference as I discovered the potential to create bold, abstract, pop-arty patterns through the application of different colouring methods, palettes, and wave manipulations.

Multiple waves with different amplitudes, wavelengths, and orientations (sometimes circular as from 'droplets'), are generated randomly, and their interference pattern is calculated. The interference pattern is then coloured by either amplitude or slope, with amplitude optionally subdivided to create the appearance of multiple nested waves. Each colour segment is shaded using a random number of contour steps, which affects the apparent smoothness of the waves.

With the optional 'striped' feature, colours in each segment are selected randomly from the image palette, which allows for both continuous and discontinues colouring of waves as they traverse the stripe boundaries.

Prompt: Made in 10 minutes

This entry for Genuary 2023, Day 2 was supposed to take 10 minutes. Turns out the idea took less than 10 minutes to sketch out, but it took more like 2 hours to fully implement. More about Genuary here: https://genuary.art/

I wanted to abstract a warp/marble type effect that I used to create textiles designs for https://glitchtextiles.com/covid-19. The concepts were things I'd templated before, and worked out in Java. Porting them over to javascript should have been fairly simple. What should have been mostly copy paste, edit, became almost a complete rebuild from scratch.

What's going on under the hood:

1. Lines are drawn, colored based on hue range. All of this randomized.
2. A band, orthogonal to the orientation of the lines, is selected for warping based on a Perlin noise function.
3. The whole piece is then warped again along the original orientation of the lines.

The piece may change with different window sizes. It's a feature, not a bug!

23093.d:
Kyma (/kee-ma/, κύμα) is a Greek word meaning wave. It is my exploration of an acoustic phenomenon known as ‘Chladni Patterns’. 

Ernst Florens Friedrich Chladni was a German physicist and musician. He was a pioneer of modern acoustics and made numerous contributions to the field. Chladni's work had a significant influence on the development of modern music theory and the technology of musical instruments. In 1787, Chladni was trying to understand how sound waves propagate and interact with objects. By vibrating a metal plate and sprinkling sand on it, he observed that the sand arranged itself into distinct patterns. These patterns are created due to the interaction between the sound waves and the plate: the sound waves cause the plate to vibrate, which in turn causes the sand to move. The sand will move away from areas of high vibration and towards areas of low vibration. This creates a unique pattern of ridges, circles, and many other shapes.

Kyma continues this study by adding color, light, and composition to the equation. Each iteration is a unique combination of two Chladni plates with different characteristics, accompanied by a palette, background lighting, and variational drawing algorithm. Plates interact with each other, forming patterns from the small detailed net-like grid to megalithic sculptures of unknown creatures and windows to another worlds.

Wandering Nets is a digital kinetic light sculpture by Matt Ebb.

Networks of light are created and connected via random walks in space and colour. Emergent structures are revealed by the ambient interaction, tension and collision of these networks within themselves and orbiting shadowed spherical bodies.

The piece is the result of several months of custom development in realtime volume rendering. The scene data is generated in javascript and rendered with a bespoke GLSL raytracer - no external libraries are used.

23175.d:
Roll the dice with shapes and capture the moment! 
Est follows Iacta which follows Alea. So here we are now: alea iacta est.

How does it work?

Each Est consists of 64 objects randomly arranged around a center and randomly differing in shape, size, texture, and movement. A curated 6 colors palette is picked and used for the textures. The color palette is sorted by hue, luminosity and/or colorfulness based on the color reference and direction variables.

The animation itself is 32 frames long and stops abruptly. It consists of 3 layers. The first layer moves the objects around the center and draws the animated objects displacing vertex positions and textures coordinates based on modulated sinus waves. Textures are additionally dithered based on a randomized fake 6x6 bayer dither matrix.

The second layer uses the first one and a double buffer to capture the motion blur based on a depth mask.

The third layer is mainly used for screen rendering, debugging and behind-the-scene looks. In addition, postprocessing is performed by shifting the drawing position based on color and center distance.

Features:

- shapes [3] (more s, more m, more l)
- palette [102] (based on YPS magazine covers (Germany), issues 700-750 / 800-850, published 1989 - 1992)
- color sort direction [2] (up, down)
- color sort reference [3] (0, 1, 2) - sorting mode selection

Animation and feature selection are based on the deterministic prng Xoshiro128 seeded with the fxhash. This allows repeated playback in the same sequence. The animation is synchronized with frames and not with time.

The preview images are taken after 32 frames.

Shortcuts & interactions:

- spacebar to trigger a rotation animation (or single click / tap)
- o to trigger random object change animation followed by a rotation animation (or double click / tap)
- r to trigger a random feature change followed by a random object change and rotation animation (or triple click / tap)
- k to enable the kiosk mode and set the speed (off, 3, 5 or 10 secs)
- m to set the kiosk mode (animate, objects, features (default), special)
- s to toggle the postprocessing screen mode (default, raw, alternative, rasterized, facetes, lineblocks, all) - experimental
- c to capture an image
- f for full screen mode
- h to see all options

Available query string parameters:

- size=8000 - sets the base size for width/height to 8000px (default 3000, useful if you want to capture bigger pngs)
- showannouncement - activates the announcement
- kioskspeed=5 - activates the kiosk mode and sets the speed in seconds

"Temporal Black" is a generative (pure code) artwork of abstract colored geometric shapes and forms, mixed in a way that trying to simulate natural media

Technically, colored shapes and curves are drawn in a graphic buffer and my custom fragment shader process and transforms the buffer content into that noisy and scratched output. All are 100% code, no images used.


CONTROLS

KEYS:

- 1-4: Set resolution from 1x to 4x of the current dimension (possibly slower performance in higher values)
- S: Save a png file with the current resolution

- P: Change orientation to Portrait with aspect ratio 0.75 (useful eg. for printing)
- L: Change orientation to Landscape with ratio 4/3  (1.333..)
- O: Change orientation to Square (box)
  Due to some 1:1 ratio sensitive calculations, rendering output may differ when switching orientations

My continued exploration of color, shape, form, function, fractal chaos, order, and understanding of the mathematical beauty of nature to create beautiful, unique and colorful designs made up of translucent glassy elements. In this piece I explore symmetry and contrasting elements, suggesting a nearly impossible blown glass sculpture. Each unique rendering has a character of its own, some smooth and sensuous while others with sharp color and form changes, ragged edges, and chaotic beauty. Interactive with several user controls:

With the mouse:

Left click and drag to change the viewing angle
Right click and drag to change the view center
Mouse wheel to change the distance to the view center

With the keyboard:

Keys "," and "." (i.e. "<" and ">") change the rotation speed left or right. You can stop it entirely, or speed it up to what I consider a reasonable maximum, rotating to the left or to the right. Each time you press, it adjusts the rotation speed

Keys "a" "b" and "c": the lights always start in the same place, and each key controls one of the three lights, both position and intensity. It is deterministic from the initial start based upon the token: for a given token, after the initial run (or re-run) pressing "aaabbcabcabc" will give you the same sequence of lighting changes. This lets you choose your favorite and keep track of it.

“Allan McCollum’s Plaster Surrogates was a thought-provoking series of sculptures that examines the role of art in contemporary society. The sculptures are cast from plaster and painted to resemble frames, mats, and black rectangles, creating a visual illusion of empty picture frames. McCollum's intention with the surrogates was to comment on the mass production and consumption of art objects, as well as the way in which art is often valued for its social function rather than its inherent aesthetic qualities.”

Continuing the integration of generative art and conceptual art, this work is a digital reproduction and inspiration of Plaster Surrogates - 1982 by noted conceptual artist, Allan McCollum.

Even though the original work had completely black rectangles, in this work, contrasting colors are used in some variations to increase the beauty. The dimensions and colors of the frames are calculated according to McCollum's original work. Various color palettes and canvas sizes have been used.

-----------

No images are used, created entirely by coding. Textures such as wood, canvas, and oil paint have been created to create a realistic look. Preview optimized for fxhash capturing system and full rendering can take up to several minutes, so I highly recommend checking out this artwork in high quality.
